prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms enabled optical frequency standards at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B049 to B008. My test in round 1 was whether a prize can be written down as a simple mechanism, established by decisive experiment, with credit that matches the record. B008 now meets that test better than my own first choice. The mechanism is a single clean idea: at the magic wavelength the lattice light shifts the two clock levels equally, so many atoms can be confined tightly without perturbing the transition. It is analytically transparent and it removes the quantum-projection-noise limit of single-ion clocks by allowing many atoms to be probed at once. It was then realised at the 10^-18 level, reproduced and surpassed by independent groups in Sr, Yb and Hg, and routinely compared internationally. That is the maturity I ask for. It also opened observables that were not accessible before, such as millimetre-scale gravitational redshift inside one sample and many-body spin-exchange effects in the clock, so it is more than a better number. Five colleagues prefer it for reasons that differ in detail but agree on the core, and I have not been given a scientific argument against it, only questions about category and overlap. I do not treat the count as the reason. The reason is that, after the first-round exchange, the credit for B008 (Katori for the idea and first Sr lattice clock, Ye for taking it to the limit and for the many-body physics) is defensible, whereas the credit for B049 is not defensible within a three-person cap.
statement.case_against: The overlap and category objections are real. The 2005 prize covered the comb and the 2012 prize covered control of single quantum systems, and a skeptic can call the lattice clock a very large improvement of an established technology rather than a discovery about nature. No deviation from standard physics has yet been found with it, so the physics reach is largely prospective, and the SI second has not been redefined. The boundary around the pair is also a judgement: SYRTE, PTB, NIST and Lemonde, Ludlow and Sterr made essential parallel or later contributions, and I cannot say from my own field whether any key systematic (blackbody shift, hyperpolarisability, density shift) was first established outside Katori and Ye. I also hold that a concept-defining discovery such as the quantum spin Hall effect or KPZ universality is, in kind, a stronger prize than a measurement capability, and I accept B008 partly because those two cannot be credited cleanly this year, not because the kinds are equal.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that Kane and Mele's 2005 papers predate the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and the 3D work, so their claim to the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall idea is earliest, and that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp form a complete core for B049.
responses.response: I accept the priority point: Kane and Mele are first on the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall concept, and I think that part of the record is secure. It does not close the gap for me, because the system in which the effect was observed was selected by the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and Kane and Mele's own graphene mechanism has a spin-orbit gap far too small to be seen. A citation naming Kane, Mele and Molenkamp therefore either implies a lineage that did not happen or must be worded so loosely that it hides the person who made the experiment possible. Zhang's death does not change the statutory problem for the living credit. You asked me to show the trio is a complete discovery, and I cannot do so within three names. That is why I have moved to B008, while keeping B049 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B008 first, says Katori's magic-wavelength idea and Ye's record performance give a clean two-person prize, and that the lattice clock has been reproduced and surpassed by independent groups with routine comparisons. She can judge the atomic-structure and systematic-shift physics directly.
responses.response: In round 1 I asked whether the novelty is a new physical principle or only a large improvement of existing technology. Your account answers it for me. The magic wavelength is a new principle, because it removes the lattice-induced shift while keeping a large number of atoms, and the quantum-projection-noise advantage follows from it. That is more than refinement of the comb or of ion control. I would still like you to answer the chair's question on whether any key systematic was first controlled outside the two names, since that decides the credit boundary and I cannot judge it. If your answer is that the shifts were established by Katori and Ye or are shared in a way that does not point to a third person, I am satisfied with the pair.

responses.point: Kroll supports B008 on experimental evidence, as reproduced by several independent laboratories, but notes that the invention can be argued as Katori's alone with Ye's contribution being performance and physics, and discloses a year in Hall's laboratory that could bear on recusal.
responses.response: I think your attribution risk is the right one to test, and I would resolve it the way you and Pearce suggest, by naming both the invention and the development in the citation. Ye's group did not merely improve a number: the many-body and spin-exchange understanding explains why the clock reaches that level, which is a physics contribution distinct from the idea. I would also note for the record that your disclosure is a personal tie to the Hall environment, with no collaboration with Katori or Ye, and I do not see it as requiring recusal, though the final decision on that is for the chair and the committee.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that a discovery of a new particle settled a half-century question and outweighs the clean attribution of the clock, and he accepts that the three-of-four choice among Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee is a judgement the record cannot settle.
responses.response: I agree that in kind the Higgs observation is a larger result than a clock, and I take your point that the 2013 prize recognised the prediction. But your own case against states the problem: any trio drops a founder with an equal claim, and no principled rule has been offered. I prefer to withhold the prize in a given year rather than make an arbitrary choice among equally valid claims. If the committee finds a rule that Lindroth, Olsson and Pearce also accept, B056 should be ranked high in a later year. For this year I do not think the attribution can bear it.

uncertainties: Whether any key lattice-clock systematic was established by a group outside Katori and Ye, which would move the credit boundary toward SYRTE, PTB, NIST or the ion-clock lineage.

Whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes make the lattice clock look like a continuation of a rewarded line to the wider Academy, and whether the citation can credibly rest on the magic-wavelength principle and demonstrated performance only.
Whether a prize for a measurement capability should rank equally with a concept-defining discovery when no deviation from standard physics has yet been found.

Whether the topological-insulator history can ever be credited fairly in three names, given Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang (deceased), the 3D contributors and the 2016 prize; I could be wrong that this is disqualifying.
My field distance: I judge the clock mainly from the statistical-physics and theory side, and rely on the atomic-physics members for the experimental systematics.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B008 or any shortlisted candidate or credited name. I remain in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Goran Johansson and Eva Olsson, with no specific collaboration, and I do not think that requires recusal. I note the disclosures by Kroll, Johansson, Olsson and Lindroth, and I have no tie to Katori, Ye or the Hall/JILA group.
